title.en: HTTP Fundamentals: The Language of the Web

description.en: Understand how browsers and servers communicate using HTTP methods, status codes, and headers.

story_variants.en:
## The Post Office of the Internet

Vaathiyaar walks into class carrying a stack of envelopes. "Every time you visit a website, your browser sends a **letter** to a server and waits for a **reply**. That letter follows strict rules — those rules are **HTTP**."

### What is HTTP?
- **H**yper**T**ext **T**ransfer **P**rotocol
- A request-response protocol between client and server
- Stateless: each request is independent
- Uses methods (verbs) to describe the action

### HTTP Methods

| Method | Purpose | Example |
|--------|---------|----------|
| `GET` | Retrieve data | Load a webpage |
| `POST` | Send data | Submit a form |
| `PUT` | Replace data | Update a profile |
| `PATCH` | Partial update | Change just the email |
| `DELETE` | Remove data | Delete an account |

### Status Codes

| Range | Meaning | Common Codes |
|-------|---------|---------------|
| `2xx` | Success | 200 OK, 201 Created |
| `3xx` | Redirect | 301 Moved, 304 Not Modified |
| `4xx` | Client Error | 400 Bad Request, 404 Not Found |
| `5xx` | Server Error | 500 Internal Server Error |

### Headers
Headers carry metadata: `Content-Type`, `Authorization`, `User-Agent`, `Accept`.

> **Key Concept:** HTTP is the foundation of ALL web communication. Every API call, every webpage load, every form submission uses HTTP.

animation_sequence.code:
import requests

response = requests.get('https://httpbin.org/get')
status = response.status_code
content_type = response.headers['Content-Type']
data = response.json()
origin = data['origin']

print(f'Type: {content_type}')
print(f'Origin: {origin}')

practice_challenges.starter_code:
import requests

# Make a GET request to httpbin
response = requests.get('https://httpbin.org/get')

# Print the status code
print(f'Status: {response.status_code}')

# Print the Content-Type header
print(f'Content-Type: {response.headers["Content-Type"]}')

# Parse JSON and print the origin IP
data = response.json()
print(f'Origin: {data["origin"]}')

under_the_hood.summary: An HTTP exchange is plain structured text sent over a TCP connection: a request line, headers, a blank line and an optional body go out, and a status line, headers, a blank line and a body come back.

steps.title: Find the server and connect
steps.body: For https://example.com/about the browser first resolves example.com to an IP address with DNS, then opens a TCP connection to port 443 and performs a TLS handshake so the rest is encrypted. Port 80 is used for plain http. Only then is any HTTP sent.

props.title: Before the first byte of HTTP

steps.title: The request is lines of text
steps.body: The first line names the method, the path and the version: GET /about HTTP/1.1. Header lines follow, such as Host: example.com, Accept: text/html and a Cookie if the browser has one. A blank line ends the headers; a POST would put its body (form fields or JSON) after it.

steps.title: The response mirrors it
steps.body: The server answers with a status line such as HTTP/1.1 200 OK, headers such as Content-Type: text/html; charset=utf-8 and Content-Length: 1256, a blank line, then exactly that many bytes of body. Content-Length (or chunked encoding) is how the client knows where the body ends.

steps.title: Status codes are grouped by first digit
steps.body: 2xx means success (200 OK, 201 Created), 3xx means look elsewhere (301 Moved Permanently with a Location header), 4xx means the client got something wrong (400, 401, 404), and 5xx means the server failed (500, 503). Clients branch on the first digit before reading anything else.

steps.title: Stateless, so cookies carry state
steps.body: Each request stands alone: the server does not remember the previous one on its own. To keep you logged in, the server sends Set-Cookie: session=abc123 once, and the browser attaches Cookie: session=abc123 to every later request to that site. HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 send the same methods, headers and status codes in binary frames, but the meaning is unchanged.

under_the_hood.takeaway: Every web feature, from forms to APIs to logins, is built from this one exchange: a method, a path, headers and maybe a body in; a status, headers and a body out.
